solution:
The equations of the parabolas are
\(y^2 = 4ax\) ... (I)
and \(x^2 = 4ay\) ... (II)
From (II) \(y = \dfrac{x^2}{4a}\) substitute in (I)
\(\left(\dfrac{x^2}{4a}\right)^2 = 4ax\)
\(\Rightarrow x^4 = 64a^3 x\)
\(\therefore x(x^3 - 64a^3) = 0\)
\(\therefore x[x^3 - (4a)^3] = 0\)
\(\therefore x = 0\) and \(x = 4a\) \(\therefore y = 0\) and \(y = 4a\)
The point of intersection of curves are \(O(0, 0)\), \(P(4a, 4a)\)
\(\therefore\) The required area is in the first quadrant and it is
A \(= \) area under the parabola (\(y^2 = 4ax\)) \(- \) area under the parabola (\(x^2 = 4ay\))
\(A = \int_{0}^{4a} \sqrt{4ax}\,dx - \int_{0}^{4a} \dfrac{x^2}{4a}\,dx = \sqrt{4a}\int_{0}^{4a} x^{1/2}\,dx - \int_{0}^{4a} \dfrac{x^2}{4a}\,dx\)
\(= 2\sqrt{a} \cdot \left[\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4a} - \dfrac{1}{4a} \cdot \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{4a}\)
\(= \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{a} \cdot \left[4a\sqrt{4a}\right] - \dfrac{1}{4a} \cdot \dfrac{64a^3}{3} = \dfrac{32}{3}a^2 - \dfrac{16}{3}a^2\)
\(\therefore A = \dfrac{16}{3}a^2\) sq. units.

Required area \(A = 2 \times\) area of OPQO
\(\therefore A = 2\int_{0}^{4} x \cdot dy\)
\(A = 2 \cdot \int_{0}^{4} \sqrt{y} \cdot dy = 2 \cdot \left[\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot y^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4} = \left(\dfrac{4}{3} \times 4^{3/2}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3} \times 8\)
\(A = \dfrac{32}{3}\) sq. units.
note: The factor 2 (two symmetric halves) was dropped from this line; the lines before and after carry it.

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed sub-part (i) gives \(x = 1,\ x = 2\), but the book's own worked solution and figure use \(x = 1\) to \(x = 3\) (area 26/3). Solved for the intended \(x \in [1, 3]\).]

Let A be the required area.
(i) \(A = \int_{1}^{3} y\,dx = \int_{1}^{3} x^2\,dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\left[x^3\right]_{1}^{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}[27 - 1]\), \(A = \dfrac{26}{3}\) sq. units.
(ii) \(A = \int_{1}^{4} y\,dx = \int_{1}^{4} 2\sqrt{x}\,dx = 2\int_{1}^{4} x^{1/2}\,dx = 2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}\left[x^{3/2}\right]_{1}^{4} = \dfrac{4}{3}\left[4^{3/2} - 1\right]\), \(A = \dfrac{28}{3}\) sq. units.
(iii) \(A = \left|\int_{-\pi/2}^{0} \sin x\,dx\right| + \left|\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin x\,dx\right| = \left|\left[-\cos x\right]_{-\pi/2}^{0}\right| + \left|\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\right| = \left|-\left[\cos 0 - \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]\right| + \left|\left[-\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \cos 0\right]\right| = |[-1 - 0]| + |[0 + 1]| = 1 + 1\), \(A = 2\) sq. units.
note: The signed integral of sin x over the interval is 0; the area is the sum of the two magnitudes, which is where the line now starts.

solution:
**Convention used.** The X-axis is named as one of the boundaries of the region, so the region is the part of the parabola's interior lying ABOVE the X-axis (the upper branch \(y=+2\sqrt{ax}\)), between \(x=0\) and \(x=a\). So only the part with \(y \geq 0\) is counted. (If instead both branches were intended, the region is symmetric about the X-axis and the area is twice the value below.)

For \(y^{2}=4ax\) with \(a>0\), the upper branch is \(y=2\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{x}\).

\(A=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}y\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}2\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{x}\,dx=2\sqrt{a}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}x^{1/2}\,dx\)

\(=2\sqrt{a}\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{a}=\dfrac{4\sqrt{a}}{3}\left(a^{3/2}-0\right)=\dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{a}\cdot a\sqrt{a}\)

\(\therefore\ A=\dfrac{4a^{2}}{3}\) sq. units.

Check by dimensions and by a special case: taking \(a=4\) gives the parabola \(y^{2}=16x\) between \(x=0\) and \(x=4\), whose upper half has area \(\int_{0}^{4}4\sqrt{x}\,dx=\dfrac{64}{3}\); the formula gives \(\dfrac{4(16)}{3}=\dfrac{64}{3}\) - the same value.
note: Replaced an internal remark about how other questions are treated.
